---
title: "Tree protection zone calculator"
description: "How much space to fence off around a tree during construction, digging or landscaping, based on trunk size, age and species tolerance."
anchor-sections: false
include-in-header: _hm-head.html
---

Most of a tree's roots are in the top 12–18 inches of soil and spread well beyond the branches. Driving, stockpiling, trenching or changing the grade over them can kill a mature tree, often a few years later. Before any work, fence off a protection zone.

**Measure the trunk** at 4½ ft (1.4 m) above the ground. Wrap a tape around it for the circumference, or measure the diameter directly.

```{=html}
<div class="hmc" id="tp"></div>
<script>
(function () {
  // Protection-zone radius as a multiple of trunk diameter, by species tolerance and age
  const F = { good: { young: 6, mature: 8, old: 12 }, mod: { young: 8, mature: 12, old: 15 }, poor: { young: 12, mature: 15, old: 18 } };
  HM.tool({
    id: 'tp', step: 'The tree',
    inputs: [
      { k: 'how', l: 'I measured the', t: 'seg', d: 'circ', opts: [['circ', 'Circumference (around)'], ['dia', 'Diameter (across)']] },
      { k: 'c', l: 'Trunk circumference', t: 'dia', show: v => v.how === 'circ' },
      { k: 'd', l: 'Trunk diameter', t: 'dia', show: v => v.how === 'dia' },
      { k: 'age', l: 'Age', t: 'select', d: 'mature', opts: [['young', 'Young (under about ⅕ of its life span)'], ['mature', 'Mature'], ['old', 'Old or in decline']] },
      { k: 'tol', l: 'How well this species tolerates root disturbance', t: 'select', d: 'mod', opts: [['good', 'Good (e.g. many maples, elms, honeylocust, willows)'], ['mod', 'Moderate or not sure'], ['poor', 'Poor (e.g. many oaks, beech, conifers, older trees in general)']], h: 'Tolerance varies with species and site. When in doubt, choose moderate or poor.' }
    ],
    compute(v, U) {
      const D = v.how === 'circ' ? (v.c > 0 ? v.c / Math.PI : null) : v.d;
      if (!(D > 0)) return U.empty('Enter the trunk measurement.');
      const f = F[v.tol][v.age], r = D * f; // metres
      const area = Math.PI * r * r, fence = 2 * Math.PI * r;
      const simple = U.us ? D / 0.0254 * 0.3048 : D * 12;
      let h = U.big('Protect a circle', `${U.f(r, 'len', 1)} radius`, `measured out from the trunk in every direction: ${U.f(2 * r, 'len', 0)} across.`);
      h += U.kv([['Trunk diameter', U.f(D, 'dia', 1)], ['Area to protect', U.f(area, 'area', 0)], ['Fencing to go around it', U.f(fence, 'len', 0)]]);
      h += `<h3>Inside the zone</h3><ul class="plain"><li>No driving, parking or storing materials, soil or equipment.</li><li>No trenching or digging. Route utilities around it, or tunnel (bore) under the roots.</li><li>No raising or lowering the grade, even by a few inches. Two inches of fill can suffocate roots.</li><li>No washing out concrete, paint or fuel.</li><li>Spread 4–6 in of wood chips inside the fence and water during dry spells.</li></ul>`;
      if (r > 15) h += U.note('That is a big zone. If work has to happen inside it, talk to a certified arborist first: there are ways to reduce damage, like root pruning in advance, ground protection mats or air-spade excavation.');
      return { html: h, work: [v.how === 'circ' ? `Diameter = circumference ÷ π = ${U.f(v.c, 'dia', 1)} ÷ 3.1416 = ${U.f(D, 'dia', 1)}` : null, `Radius = ${f} × diameter (${v.tol === 'good' ? 'good' : v.tol === 'mod' ? 'moderate' : 'poor'} tolerance, ${v.age} tree) = ${f} × ${U.f(D, 'dia', 1)} = ${U.f(r, 'len', 1)}`, `For comparison, the simple rule of 1 ft of radius per inch of diameter gives ${U.f(U.us ? D / 0.0254 * 0.3048 : D * 12, 'len', 1)}`, `Area = π × r² = ${U.f(area, 'area', 0)}; fence = 2 × π × r = ${U.f(fence, 'len', 0)}`].filter(Boolean) };
    }
  });
})();
</script>
```

## Why trees die after construction

Roots need air as much as water. Compaction from vehicles crushes the pore spaces; fill soil buries roots too deep; trenching cuts them. The tree may look fine for a season or two, using stored energy, then decline from the top down. By the time you see dieback, the damage was done years before.

The zone here scales with the trunk, the tree's age and how well the species copes, following a widely used arborist approach. The simpler rule of thumb, one foot of radius per inch of trunk diameter, is shown in the working for comparison.
